definition: Cursory means so quick and surface-level that it stops at a glance — brief to the point of being superficial.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cursory. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cursory should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One cursory sweep of the flashlight satisfied the night guard, who signed the log and never saw the open window on the mezzanine.
Quick is weaker than cursory: a quick check is merely fast and can still be sharp, while a cursory one is so shallow it never gets beneath the surface.
Perfunctory goes further than cursory: a cursory glance at least tries to see something, while a perfunctory one is empty routine, performed only so the box can be ticked.
Hurried means done at speed because the clock demands it — a hurried job can still be careful in what it touches. Cursory adds the real charge: the attention itself never leaves the surface.

Passing describes a look that is brief because the attention is already on its way to something else — a passing glance takes in whatever it happens to catch. Cursory describes that same shallowness in a place where a real look was owed.

Cursory means so quick and surface-level that it stops at a glance — brief to the point of being superficial.
Dad's cursory check of the twins' homework — a nod at each worksheet while stirring the sauce — missed that half the answers were in the same handwriting on both papers.
The check happened, but only at the surface: a glance in passing, attention mostly elsewhere, nothing examined closely enough to catch what a real look would have caught.
That fast, shallow pass — brief to the point of being superficial — is exactly what cursory names.
Cursory is a quiet criticism: it says the look was too brief to be worth much.
Brief and quick are neutral about quality; cursory is not — a cursory reading is one that failed to really read.
And don't confuse it with cursive, the flowing joined handwriting: the two share the Latin 'running' root and nothing else.

The auction house needed an answer by Friday, so the young appraiser gave the painting what she later admitted was a cursory examination.
She checked the signature, noted the period frame, and photographed the front.
She never turned the canvas over.
The buyer's expert did, three weeks later, and found a customs stamp from a country the painter never visited.
The sale collapsed, and with it a measure of the house's reputation.
Pinned above the appraiser's desk now is a card with four words on it: 'Turn the painting over.'
